subject: biology

items.q: Two taxonomists disagree about whether a group of beetles should be ranked as a family or as a subfamily. Which statement best explains why such disagreements arise?
items.correct: The ranks are arbitrary levels imposed on a continuous gradation of variation among organisms.
items.misconception: One of the two taxonomists must be wrong, because the rank of a group is a fixed natural property.
items.why: The hierarchy is learned as a fixed ladder with a mnemonic, and every organism is given a rank at each level, so students assume the levels are discovered rather than assigned. A fixed ranking of taxa is arbitrary because it does not reflect the gradation of variation among organisms: the ranks above species are conventions chosen by taxonomists, which is one reason cladistics uses unranked clades instead.
items.specStatementText: Why the ranked hierarchy does not fit evolution
items.random_wrong: The beetles cannot be a natural group, because a true clade fits exactly one rank.

items.q: Cladistics classifies organisms into unranked clades. Why is the change from the traditional ranked hierarchy to cladistics described as a paradigm shift?
items.correct: It replaces the assumption of fixed ranks with a different framework of nested clades.
items.misconception: It draws the same ranked hierarchy of kingdom, phylum and class in a new, tree-shaped form.
items.why: Both systems are taught as ways of grouping organisms, and some cladograms in textbooks are labelled with familiar rank names, so students merge the two into one scheme. Cladistics uses unranked clades: a clade is defined by common ancestry alone, and the number of nested clades between a species and the root can be any number. Replacing fixed ranks with unranked clades is an example of a paradigm shift in classification.
items.specStatementText: Why the ranked hierarchy does not fit evolution
items.random_wrong: It replaces hypotheses with facts, because cladograms are built from DNA sequence data.

items.q: A newly discovered plant species is placed, on the basis of DNA base sequences, in a clade in which every known member produces a particular alkaloid. What can be concluded about the new species?
items.correct: It is likely to produce the alkaloid, a trait shared by descent within the clade.
items.misconception: It will resemble the other members in appearance, because that is how the clade was defined.
items.why: Identification keys and earlier courses sort organisms by visible features, and everyday classification of objects is done by appearance, so similarity is assumed to be the basis of biological classification too. The ideal classification follows evolutionary relationships: all the members of a taxonomic group should have evolved from a common ancestor. Shared appearance is only evidence of relationship, and it can mislead where similar features have evolved independently.
items.specStatementText: Why grouping by ancestry is the ideal
items.random_wrong: Nothing can be predicted until its morphology has been compared with that of the others.

items.q: Birds and crocodiles share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with lizards. The traditional class Reptilia includes crocodiles and lizards but excludes birds. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Traditional Reptilia is not a clade, because it omits some descendants of its common ancestor.
items.misconception: Reptilia is a clade, because all of its members share scales and a similar body plan, unlike birds.
items.why: The word 'group' is used loosely in earlier courses, and the definition of a clade emphasises shared characteristics, so students drop the requirement that the group must contain every descendant of one ancestor. A clade is a group of organisms that have evolved from a common ancestor, and it must include all of that ancestor's descendants. Shared characteristics are evidence for a clade only when they were inherited from the common ancestor, not when they evolved independently.
items.specStatementText: A clade is an ancestor plus all its descendants
items.random_wrong: Reptilia is a clade, because it is an established class in the traditional hierarchy.

items.q: In a comparison of one protein, species P and Q differ at 6 amino acid positions, P and R differ at 18, and Q and R differ at 18. Which conclusion is justified?
items.correct: R's lineage separated from the lineage leading to P and Q before P and Q split from each other.
items.misconception: R has changed three times as much as P has since the two lineages separated from their common ancestor.
items.why: Comparisons are usually presented against one reference species, such as humans, which is treated as unchanged, so the other species appears to have done all the changing. Since divergence, both lineages have been accumulating substitutions independently, so the differences between two living species are shared between two lineages. Divergence time is estimated from the differences per lineage, and both species have changed by a similar amount since their common ancestor.
items.specStatementText: Sequence differences accumulate, so they estimate divergence time
items.random_wrong: R is the most primitive of the three species, because its lineage was the first to diverge.

items.q: Six bases of the same gene were sequenced in four species: W is ACTGCG, X is ACTATG, Y is GTAGCG and Z is GTAATG. Using parsimony analysis, which cladogram is the most probable?
items.correct: W with X and Y with Z, because that tree accounts for all the variation with only 7 base changes.
items.misconception: W with Y and X with Z, because W and Y share the same bases at positions 4 and 5.
items.why: Class examples use very short sequences in which one position is often enough, so students stop at the first pattern they notice instead of totalling changes over all positions. Cladograms are constructed from whole sequences, and parsimony analysis selects the tree that requires the smallest total number of sequence changes. A tree favoured by one position may be rejected because it needs more changes at other positions.
items.random_wrong: All four species branching from a single node, because that tree has the fewest nodes.

items.q: What does a node on a cladogram represent?
items.correct: The hypothetical common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it.
items.misconception: A named living or fossil species from which the later lineages are descended.
items.why: Trees are read like family trees, where every junction is a real named person, and some evolutionary diagrams in earlier courses draw fossil species at the branch points. A node represents a hypothetical common ancestor; the cladogram is a hypothesis about the order in which lineages diverged, and the ancestor at each node is inferred, not observed. The living species appear only at the ends of the terminal branches.
items.random_wrong: The point at which one lineage became more advanced than the other lineage.

items.q: On a cladogram, the root leads to node 1, where species P branches off. Node 2 separates species Q from the remaining species. Node 3 separates species R from species S and T, which are joined at node 4. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: R shares a more recent common ancestor with S than it shares with Q.
items.misconception: Q is more closely related to R than to T, because Q and R branch at adjacent nodes.
items.why: In tables, keys and lists, closeness in position means closeness in category, and students read the row of tips on a cladogram in the same way. Evolutionary relationships are deduced from the nodes: species that share a more recent common ancestor are more closely related, whatever the order of the terminal branches. Each node can be rotated, so a diagram can be redrawn with the tips in a different order and mean exactly the same thing.
items.random_wrong: P is the most primitive of the five species, because it branches off nearest the root.

items.q: Several genera were placed in the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae) because of similarities in flower structure. Cladistic analysis of base sequences later showed that some of these genera are more closely related to plants in other families than to the remaining figworts, and they were transferred out of the family. Which conclusion is justified?
items.correct: The floral similarities arose by convergent evolution, so the family was not a clade and its original classification has been falsified.
items.misconception: The transferred genera must still share an ancestor with the figworts, because such similar flowers could not have evolved twice.
items.why: Students treat similar structures as a fingerprint of shared descent and underestimate how often natural selection produces similar solutions independently; the revision of families is rarely discussed before IB. Similarities in morphology may be due to convergent evolution rather than common ancestry. In the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae), floral similarities led to genera being grouped together that cladistic analysis of sequences has shown are not a clade, and they were transferred to other families.
items.specStatementText: Cladistics can show a classification is wrong
items.random_wrong: Flower structure is directly observable and so more reliable than sequences, which makes the transfer premature.

items.q: Which evidence was used in 1977 to propose that all organisms should be classified into three domains?
items.correct: Comparison of the base sequences of ribosomal RNA across many different organisms.
items.misconception: Visible differences in cell structure seen using the electron microscope.
items.why: Every earlier division of life met by students, plant against animal and prokaryote against eukaryote, was based on visible cell structure, so the same is assumed for domains, and archaea and bacteria look alike under the microscope. The three-domain classification was proposed from evidence from rRNA base sequences, not from morphology: archaea and bacteria are not distinguishable by nucleus or cell size, and only sequence comparison revealed the depth of the split between them.
items.specStatementText: Three domains, from ribosomal RNA sequences
items.random_wrong: Evidence that archaea are a subgroup of bacteria, so that all prokaryotes form one domain.

items.q: The rRNA base sequences of an archaean are found to differ from those of bacteria as much as they differ from those of eukaryotes. Which classification does this evidence support?
items.correct: Archaea as a separate domain, distinct from both Bacteria and Eukarya.
items.misconception: Archaea placed within the domain Bacteria, since both groups lack a nucleus.
items.why: Earlier courses divide life into prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and the older name 'archaebacteria' contains 'bacteria', so the prokaryote category is assumed to be a natural group. All organisms are classified into three domains, Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, using evidence from rRNA base sequences. Lacking a nucleus is a condition shared by two domains, not evidence that they form one group.
items.specStatementText: Three domains, from ribosomal RNA sequences
items.random_wrong: Archaea as a sixth kingdom, the highest level of classification.

items.q: What is the main advantage of a classification in which every group corresponds to evolutionary relationships?
items.correct: Characteristics of members of a group can be predicted.
items.misconception: The groups show which of the organisms are the most advanced.
items.why: Popular images of a march of progress from ape to human, and the habit of drawing mammals or humans at the far right of trees, suggest that evolution is a ladder rather than a branching process. A classification corresponding to evolutionary relationships is a nested set of clades, each defined by a common ancestor. Its advantage is that characteristics can be predicted within a clade; it makes no claim that any species is higher or more advanced than another.
items.specStatementText: Why grouping by ancestry is the ideal
items.random_wrong: Every species is given a unique name made up of two parts.

items.q: The same protein in two living species differs at 8 amino acid positions. Substitutions in this protein occur at about 1 per 5 million years in each lineage. Which is the best estimate of the time since the two species diverged from their common ancestor?
items.correct: About 20 million years, since roughly half of the differences have accumulated in each of the two lineages.
items.misconception: Exactly 20 million years, because the substitution rate is the same in every lineage at all times.
items.why: The name 'molecular clock' suggests the regularity of a mechanical clock, and worked examples in class give a single numerical answer without an error range. The gradual accumulation of sequence differences is the basis for estimates of divergence times, and the method can only give estimates: the rate of accumulation depends on generation time, population size, selective pressure and other factors that differ between lineages and over time.
items.specStatementText: Sequence differences accumulate, so they estimate divergence time
items.random_wrong: About 40 million years, because 8 substitutions at 5 million years each took 40 million years to occur.

items.q: Does every group in the traditional hierarchy consist of organisms that all evolved from one common ancestor?
items.correct: No. The traditional hierarchy was built largely on morphology before evolutionary relationships were known, and it does not always correspond to patterns of divergence generated by evolution; some traditional taxa exclude descendants of the group's common ancestor or combine unrelated lineages.
items.misconception: Because the hierarchy is drawn as a branching tree, every kingdom, phylum, class, order and family must already be a natural group descended from a single common ancestor.
items.why: Textbooks draw the Linnaean hierarchy as a branching diagram that looks like an evolutionary tree, and familiar taxon names such as 'reptiles' and 'fish' are used as if they were evolutionary units. The traditional hierarchy does not always correspond to patterns of divergence: a group such as the reptiles as traditionally defined omits birds, which descend from the same ancestor. Cladistics tests whether a named group is a clade instead of assuming that it is.
items.specStatementText: Why the ranked hierarchy does not fit evolution

items.q: What does parsimony analysis select among alternative cladograms?
items.correct: The cladogram in which the observed sequence variation between the clades is accounted for with the smallest number of sequence changes. It is selected as the most probable hypothesis, not proved correct.
items.misconception: The most parsimonious cladogram is the one with the simplest shape, that is, the fewest nodes and branches.
items.why: Parsimony is explained as 'the simplest explanation', and students apply 'simplest' to the appearance of the diagram rather than to the number of evolutionary changes it requires. Parsimony compares alternative branching hypotheses by counting the sequence changes each requires to explain the data; the tree needing the fewest changes is preferred. A tree with fewer nodes is not simpler in this sense and usually requires more changes.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the species at the far end of a cladogram, or the one whose lineage passes the most nodes, the most highly evolved?
items.correct: No. All the living species at the tips have been evolving for the same length of time since the root, and the number of nodes on a path depends only on how many other species happen to be included in the diagram. A cladogram shows branching order, not degree of advancement.
items.misconception: The species whose terminal branch is furthest from the root, or whose lineage passes through the most nodes, is the most advanced, and the species that branches off first is the most primitive.
items.why: The ladder image of evolution, and the convention of drawing humans or the most familiar species on the right, make a tree look like a progression. A node is a branching point, not a step upward. Species that branch off near the root are not ancestral to the others and are not primitive; they are equally modern lineages that separated early. Cladograms show common ancestry and clades, not rankings.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an established classification be shown to be wrong?
items.correct: Yes. A classification is a scientific knowledge claim and may be falsified by new evidence. The traditional figwort family was reorganised after cladistic analysis showed that it did not correspond to evolutionary relationships; theories and other knowledge claims may eventually be falsified.
items.misconception: Once taxonomists have placed a group in a family or order, that placement is an established fact that later research cannot overturn.
items.why: Classification is met in earlier courses as a finished list to be memorised, with none of the disputes or revisions shown, so it looks like a settled body of fact rather than a set of hypotheses. Theories and other scientific knowledge claims may eventually be falsified. Cladistics provides a test: if the members of a named group do not form a clade, the classification is revised, as happened with the Scrophulariaceae.
items.specStatementText: Cladistics can show a classification is wrong
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are domains simply a new name for kingdoms?
items.correct: No. Domain is an extra taxonomic level introduced above the kingdoms: each domain contains one or more kingdoms. The three-domain system did not rename the kingdoms; it added a higher level based on rRNA sequences.
items.misconception: The three domains replaced the kingdoms, so 'domain' is just the modern name for the highest groups, and the kingdoms no longer exist.
items.why: Students meet the kingdoms first and then hear that the three domains were a revolutionary reclassification, and assume the newer scheme threw the older one out. The classification of all organisms into three domains is a reclassification with an extra taxonomic level above kingdoms, proposed in 1977. Kingdoms remain within the domains, for example the plant, animal and fungal kingdoms within Eukarya.
items.specStatementText: Three domains, from ribosomal RNA sequences
